who: a red fox mother with a litter of kits at a den mouth
place: a hedgerow den at dusk in early summer, the light almost gone
present: four kits at the den mouth
one kit that has wandered ten yards into open pasture
a hawk-shaped shadow that crossed overhead twice in the last hour

factors.fact: She has not eaten since the previous night and is weak with hunger.
A hawk crossed low over the field twice in the last hour.
The straying kit is the smallest and slowest of the litter.
She can reach the straying kit in a few seconds at a run.
The den is close enough that a short dash leaves the other kits unwatched only briefly.
Kits that stray from cover rarely survive a hawk's stoop.

could_also.verb: barks a warning from the den

would_not.why: one kit lost now costs more than the risk of a short dash to fetch it
there is no time to move four kits before the hawk returns

then: She grips the kit by the scruff and carries it back to the den, then noses the others deeper into the earth before finally going off to hunt.
why: The hawk's passes make open ground dangerous right now, and this kit is both closest to danger and least able to save itself, so recovering it outweighs the hunger that would send her hunting immediately.
turns_on: whether the hawk is still circling nearby

who: a mother alone in a one-room house with her infant son
place: a cold house past midnight, the nearest healer a two-hour walk away
present: the infant, feverish and limp
a banked fire burning low
a jug of water

factors.fact: The infant's fever has climbed since sundown and his breathing rattles.
No one is expected to come check on her before morning.
She has cooled a fever before with wet cloths and it worked.
The road to the healer crosses open country with no one to help if she stumbles carrying him.
She still has clean water and cloth in the house.
He is her only child.

does.verb: stays and sponges him with cool water

could_also.verb: wraps him and sets out for the healer

would_not.verb: leaves him to fetch help alone
would_not.why: an infant this feverish cannot be left unwatched even briefly
the fever is worsening, not holding steady, so waiting risks losing him

then: She keeps sponging him through the night; toward dawn the fever breaks and his breathing eases, and only then does she send a neighbor's boy running for the healer to be sure.
why: The night road is a real danger to attempt alone with a limp child, and she has a remedy that has worked before, so she tries it first rather than risking both of them on a dark walk.
turns_on: whether the fever breaks before dawn or keeps climbing

who: a hen with a brood of chicks in a farmyard
place: an open farmyard at midday with thin cover
present: eight chicks scattered across open ground
a hawk circling high overhead
a low woodpile ten feet away

factors.fact: The hawk is circling high and has not yet folded its wings to dive.
Hens give a sharp alarm note the moment a hawk stoops, not before.
She can reach the woodpile faster than she can gather every scattered chick.
The chicks are too young to recognize the danger without her cue.
She is the only adult bird in the yard.

would_not.why: a false alarm this early would scatter the brood for nothing and teach them to ignore her call
leaving now would strand every chick with no warning at all if the hawk does dive

then: The hawk drifts off toward the treeline without diving, and she resumes scratching the ground, clucking the chicks back around her.
why: A circling hawk is not yet a stooping hawk, and false alarms cost her the chicks' trust in the real one, so she waits for the fold of the wings before committing to a call that will scatter them.
turns_on: whether the hawk folds its wings to dive

who: a wolf pup whose mother was killed by a rival pack two days ago
place: the pack's rendezvous site in late autumn, prey scarce
present: three adult wolves that are not the pup's parents
the pup's two litter-mates, thin and calling
a half-eaten carcass from the last hunt

factors.fact: None of the surviving adults is this pup's parent.
Prey has been scarce all week and the last kill barely fed the adults.
This pack has raised orphaned litters before when food allowed.
The carcass has enough left for the adults or for the pups, not comfortably both.
The pup is too young to hunt or travel with the pack.
A pup left behind at the rendezvous site alone will not survive the week.

does.verb: lets it feed at the carcass

could_also.verb: drives it off from the carcass
carries it along on the next hunt

would_not.why: the pack has never done this to an orphaned pup even when lean, and its litter-mates are watching

would_not.verb: feeds it before its own litter-mates
would_not.why: the pup is one of three at the carcass and no one of them is owed to eat first

then: The orphan feeds alongside the litter-mates, thinner than the rest but fed, and stays close to the rendezvous site through the following weeks while the adults hunt.
why: Prey is scarce but not gone, and the pack's habit of raising orphaned litters when food allows outweighs the small cost of one more mouth at a carcass that already has enough.
turns_on: whether the carcass has enough left over for a fourth mouth

who: two mature rams from the same flock in the autumn rut
place: a hillside pasture with the flock's ewes grazing nearby
present: a ewe in season
the rest of the flock grazing at a distance
the shepherd's dog resting near the gate

factors.fact: The larger ram already drove this same rival off two days earlier.
The smaller ram is limping slightly from an old injury.
The ewe will only be in season for another day or so.
The larger ram has held this flock's ewes for three seasons running.

would_not.why: he already lost this contest two days ago and his leg has not improved since
backing off from one ewe does not mean abandoning the whole flock for the season

then: He retreats to the edge of the pasture and grazes alone while the larger ram stays with the ewe, though he will test the larger ram again once his leg is sound.
why: He lost the same contest days ago against the same rival and his injury has only made him weaker since, so pressing the fight now would cost him more than the one missed chance is worth.
turns_on: whether his leg has healed since the last contest

who: a father teaching his young son to split kindling
place: a woodshed behind the house on a cold morning
present: a hatchet
a stack of unsplit wood
the boy's cut hand

factors.fact: The boy has just cut the side of his hand on the hatchet's edge.
The cut is shallow and has already stopped bleeding heavily.
This is the boy's first time handling the hatchet alone.
A shallow cut like this needs only cleaning and a wrap, not a healer.
In this house a child who is hurt learning a tool is expected to keep going once tended, not be excused from it.

could_also.verb: takes the hatchet away for good
sends him inside to his mother

would_not.verb: ignores the cut and keeps drilling him
would_not.why: an unwashed cut left untreated can fester even if it looks minor now

would_not.verb: forbids him from ever touching the hatchet again
would_not.why: one shallow cut on a first try is not reason enough to undo the lesson entirely

then: He wraps the hand, has the boy watch him split the next few logs, then hands the hatchet back once the boy's grip steadies.
why: The cut is minor and the boy needs to learn this tool sometime, so tending the hand and continuing the lesson serves him better than either ignoring the injury or ending the lesson over it.
turns_on: how deep the cut turns out to be

who: a stray cat nursing a litter of four kittens
place: a gap beneath a barn floor in a hard winter, several days since her last meal
present: four kittens, eyes barely open
a rat hole at the far end of the barn
the barn owner's boots heard outside

factors.fact: She has not caught anything in three days and her milk is thinning.
The kittens cannot yet move or feed themselves.
Leaving the nest means the kittens are unguarded and cold without her body heat.
There is a rat hole close enough to reach in a short trip.
The barn owner sometimes leaves scraps near the door but has also chased her off before.

could_also.verb: stays with the kittens and goes without
moves the litter to a new spot
goes toward the barn owner for scraps

would_not.verb: abandons the nest for the night
would_not.why: the kittens would chill badly without her within an hour in this cold
he has chased her off before and she cannot risk being driven away from the litter

then: She is back at the rat hole and returns within minutes, and though the catch is small it is enough to keep her milk going another day.
why: Her milk is failing and the kittens cannot survive on nothing, so a short, close hunt is worth the brief risk of leaving them, while a longer trip toward the barn owner's unreliable scraps is not.
turns_on: how close the nearest thing to catch is

who: a pigeon whose mate was struck by a hawk this morning
place: a ledge on a barn roof overlooking a farmyard
present: the injured mate, wing held wrong, on the ground below
a nest with no eggs yet
the hawk perched at a distance in a bare tree

factors.fact: The mate was struck minutes ago and cannot fly back up to the ledge.
The hawk that struck it is still perched nearby, watching.
This pair has nested together for two seasons.
Pigeons on the ground cannot defend against a hawk the way they can in the air.

does.verb: drops down and stays close to

could_also.verb: leaves to find a new mate

would_not.why: a pigeon has no way to drive off a hawk and would likely be struck as well

would_not.verb: abandons the mate on the ground
would_not.why: two seasons paired together outweighs the risk of standing nearby while the hawk is still just watching

then: It stays beside the injured mate until the hawk eventually loses interest and flies off, then both make their way back to the ledge on foot and wing over the next hour.
why: The hawk is watching but not yet stooping again, and the bond from two seasons together makes staying close worth more than the small risk, while attacking the hawk outright would help no one.
turns_on: whether the hawk is still watching or has moved on

who: a dairy cow whose calf is being weaned
place: a farmyard with the calf penned separately for the first time
present: the calf in an adjoining pen
a fence between them
the farmer nearby with a bucket

factors.fact: The calf has nursed from her every day since birth two months ago.
The farmer weans calves at this age every year without trouble.
The fence is solid and she cannot reach the calf through it.
The calf is old enough to take feed from a bucket now.

does.verb: paces and calls at the fence

could_also.verb: tries to break through the fence

would_not.why: the fence holds and repeated charges would only injure her for no gain
two months of daily nursing does not end the moment a fence goes up between them

then: She calls and paces at the fence for the first day, then gradually settles as the calf takes to the bucket and the distance becomes routine.
why: The bond from two months of nursing does not vanish just because a fence appears, but the fence holds and the calf is genuinely ready for the bucket, so distress rather than escape is what follows.
turns_on: how many days since the pen went up

who: a yearling bear cub whose mother has wandered out of sight while foraging
place: a berry slope in late summer, the mother's scent trail nearby but the cub cannot see her
present: a patch of ripe berries
a fallen log with grubs under the bark
the mother's scent trail leading away

factors.fact: The cub is hungry and the berries here are ripe and close.
This is the first time it has been out of sight of its mother.
It knows how to follow a scent trail, though it has never done so alone.
It has never fed itself for more than a few minutes without her nearby.

would_not.why: straying further would make it much harder to find her scent again
running without a direction only increases the chance of getting properly lost

then: It eats quickly, glancing up often, and when a twig snaps nearby it abandons the berries and trots off along her scent trail until it finds her a few minutes later.
why: The hunger and the easy food in front of it are real, but never having been alone this long makes it stay close enough to the scent trail that a sudden sound sends it straight back to searching for her.
turns_on: whether a sound startles it while it is feeding

who: a mother with a toddler and a newborn
place: a farmyard with an open well, midmorning
present: the newborn, crying and needing to be fed
the toddler, wandering toward the well's low wall
the well itself, uncovered

factors.fact: The newborn has been crying to be fed for several minutes.
The toddler is now within a few steps of the well's edge.
She cannot carry both children to safety in one motion.
The toddler has climbed onto the well's low wall before and been pulled down for it.

does.verb: drops the newborn onto bedding and runs to

would_not.why: the newborn crying is uncomfortable but not in danger, while the well is a fall away from something far worse
the toddler has climbed the wall before and a shout alone did not stop it that time

then: She scoops the toddler off the wall, sets them both down away from the well, and only then goes back to settle and feed the crying newborn.
why: A crying newborn is safe where it lies, but a toddler beside an open well is one misstep from drowning, so the well outweighs the crying every time this choice comes up.
turns_on: how close the toddler already is to the well's edge

who: an elephant calf whose mother died of illness two days ago
place: open grassland where the herd is moving toward new water
present: the herd's matriarch and several other females
the calf's own aunt, who has a calf of similar age
the herd's slow travel pace

factors.fact: The calf's aunt already has a calf of her own to nurse.
The orphan can still keep pace with the herd's slow travel for now.
This herd has adopted orphaned calves before when one female had milk to spare.
The orphan cannot yet feed itself on grass alone at this age.
The matriarch decides where and how fast the herd moves.

does.verb: lets it walk alongside and nurse

could_also.verb: drives it away from her own calf
leaves it behind with the herd
the matriarch slows the herd for it

would_not.why: the herd has taken in orphans before and this aunt has milk enough to share for now
a calf this age left alone on open grassland will not survive predators or thirst

then: The orphan nurses alongside its cousin and keeps pace with the herd for now, though it will need the aunt's tolerance to hold for months before it can feed itself.
why: The aunt has milk enough to spare and the herd's custom favors taking in an orphan it can still keep up with, so tolerance costs less now than the calf's death would cost later.
turns_on: whether the aunt's own milk holds out for two

who: a male sparrow courting a hen that is already paired
place: a hedge nesting site in early spring
present: the paired hen
her mate, currently away foraging
a half-built nest in the hedge

factors.fact: Her mate left to forage only moments ago and has not returned.
A paired hen this early in nest-building rarely accepts another male.
This male has already been driven off by her mate once this season.
It is still early enough in spring that unpaired hens can still be found elsewhere.

could_also.verb: waits nearby for the mate to leave again

would_not.verb: stays to fight the mate for her
would_not.why: he has already lost that fight once this season and the mate is due back any moment
a hen already committed to a nest this early is very unlikely to leave it for him

then: He gives up within a minute when the mate's call sounds nearby, and flies off to try his luck with an unpaired hen two hedges over.
why: The hen is unlikely to leave a nest she has already started, and he has already lost the fight for her once, so a brief attempt and a quick retreat cost him less than staying to be driven off again.
turns_on: whether the mate returns before he gives up

who: a herding dog guarding a pen of young goats
place: a pen at the edge of pasture at night, two jackals circling
present: a dozen young goats in the pen
two jackals circling just outside the fence
the shepherd asleep in a hut some distance off

factors.fact: There are two jackals, and the dog has only ever driven off one at a time before.
The pen fence is intact and the jackals have not yet found a gap.
The dog has guarded this pen every night for three years.
Leaving the pen to chase one jackal would let the other approach unguarded.

would_not.verb: chases one jackal into the dark
would_not.why: leaving the fence line would let the second jackal in while it is occupied with the first

would_not.verb: abandons the pen to fetch the shepherd
would_not.why: the fence is still holding and leaving now would hand the jackals an unguarded pen

then: It holds its ground barking until the noise and its refusal to break position discourage both jackals, which drift off before dawn without breaching the fence.
why: Two jackals is more than it has handled alone before, but the fence is still whole, and chasing either one away from the line would open the pen to the other, so holding position outweighs pursuit.
turns_on: whether the fence has an actual gap they can use

who: a woman whose husband went out fishing and has not returned
place: a fishing village cottage, three days since the boat should have come back
present: their young child, asking where their father is
neighbors who have stopped mentioning it
the boat's usual mooring, empty

factors.fact: Boats caught in the same storm three days ago have washed up empty before, with no survivors found after this long.
They have been married since before the child was born.
The child still needs to be fed, dressed and told something.
The village expects mourning to begin once hope is clearly gone, not before.

does.verb: keeps watching the water and waiting

could_also.verb: tells the child he is not coming back
asks neighbors to search further out

would_not.verb: begins mourning outright on day three
would_not.why: three days is within the range boats have returned late before, so it is too soon by the village's own reckoning

would_not.verb: tells the child nothing at all
would_not.why: the child is already asking and needs some honest answer, not silence

then: She tells the child only that the sea has kept him longer than usual, and keeps the fire lit and food ready in case the boat comes in after dark.
why: Three days is grim but not yet past the point where boats from that storm have returned, so the village's own custom and her own hope both say to keep watching a little longer before mourning begins.
turns_on: how many days since the boat was due back

who: a wild rabbit with a litter of kits in a shallow burrow
place: a warren entrance at dawn, a fox's scent fresh nearby
present: five healthy kits
one kit, weak and barely moving, that has soiled the nest
fresh fox scent at the warren's mouth

factors.fact: A fox has scented near this warren entrance within the last hour.
A weak, soiled kit draws predators to the whole nest faster than a clean one.
The other five kits are healthy and likely to survive if the nest is not found.
She cannot clean or save the weak kit fast enough to remove the scent it has already left.

could_also.verb: cleans the nest and kit thoroughly

would_not.verb: stays to nurse the weak kit through it
would_not.why: the scent it is already leaving is the more urgent danger to the five healthy kits, and nursing will not stop that
moving five kits at dawn with a fox already close by is more dangerous than removing the one already failing

then: She carries the weak kit out and leaves it some distance from the warren, then returns to groom the remaining nest thoroughly before settling back over the five that remain.
why: The weak kit's scent is already a danger to five healthy siblings, and there is no time to both save it and remove that danger, so the five outweigh the one that was least likely to survive regardless.
turns_on: how strong the fox's scent is at the warren mouth

who: a shepherd and his young daughter, delivering a ewe's first lamb
place: a lambing shed at night in early spring
present: the straining ewe
a lamb with a leg bent back inside her
a lantern giving poor light

factors.fact: The father has felt a leg bent back like this before and knows it can be turned by hand.
The ewe is tiring and cannot push much longer without help.
This is the daughter's first time helping with a difficult birth.
The daughter's hands are smaller and can reach further inside than his.

does.verb: guides his daughter's hand to turn

could_also.verb: sends for a neighbor with more experience
lets the ewe labor on unaided

would_not.verb: lets the ewe labor on unaided
would_not.why: she is already tiring and a bent leg like this will not correct itself
the nearest help is too far away and the ewe does not have that much time left

then: Guided by his voice, the daughter reaches in and turns the leg straight, and the lamb slides free minutes later, wet and breathing, while the ewe rests.
why: He has felt this kind of trouble before and knows it can be fixed by hand, and his daughter's smaller hands can do it more easily than his own, so teaching her in the moment serves the ewe better than either waiting or doing it himself.
turns_on: whether the leg can be reached and turned in time

who: a stray dog nursing a litter of puppies in a cold alley
place: a sheltered alcove behind a shop in winter
present: five puppies, a few days old
a person crouching nearby with food and a warm bag
the alcove's thin shelter from the wind

factors.fact: She has not eaten today and the food being offered is close and real.
The person's hands are reaching toward one of the puppies, not just setting food down.
People in this alley have thrown things at her before, though this one has not.
The puppies are only a few days old and cannot survive being separated from her yet.

could_also.verb: takes the food while watching the person
retreats deeper into the alcove with the puppies

would_not.verb: lets the puppy be picked up without protest
would_not.why: a puppy this young separated from her would not survive the cold or the lack of milk

would_not.verb: abandons the food to attack outright
would_not.why: the person has not actually hurt her and biting would risk being driven off from her own shelter

then: She stands her ground until the person withdraws the reaching hand, then eats the food once left alone, keeping the puppies pulled close against her side.
why: The food is worth taking but not at the cost of a puppy being taken, and past experience with people in this alley makes her wary rather than trusting, even toward one who has not yet hurt her.
turns_on: whether the hand actually closes on a puppy

who: a young stallion challenging the herd's older stallion for its mares
place: an open range at the start of the breeding season
present: a band of mares grazing
the older stallion, scarred from past fights
a stretch of open ground between them

factors.fact: The young stallion is heavier and faster than the older one this season.
The older stallion won every challenge against younger males the previous two seasons.
The older stallion has held this band of mares for four years.
The young stallion has no mares of his own and the breeding season will not wait.

could_also.verb: tries to steal a mare without a direct fight
backs down at the first display

would_not.why: this season he is genuinely bigger and faster than the older stallion, unlike the seasons he lost before
waiting costs him this breeding season entirely for an advantage he already has now

then: The two fight hard for several minutes; the young stallion's extra speed wins out, and the older stallion withdraws, leaving the band to the challenger.
why: Past losses no longer reflect the two horses' current condition, and the young stallion's real physical edge this season outweighs the older stallion's years of holding the band, so the challenge is worth the risk now.
turns_on: which stallion is actually stronger this season

who: a mother sitting beside her infant, who died two days ago
place: a small house in summer heat, three days since the child died
present: other family members, waiting outside the room
the infant's body, kept in the coolest corner
the summer heat building through the day

factors.fact: In this heat, a body kept unburied this long draws sickness and cannot be preserved much longer.
This was her first child, born after several years of trying.
Custom allows a short private time before burial, but not an open-ended one.
The family waiting outside has already asked once, gently, when she will allow the burial.

could_also.verb: allows the family to proceed with burial
asks for one more night first

would_not.why: the heat and the body's condition make delay past a day or two genuinely harmful, not just against custom

would_not.verb: hands the child over without any private time at all
would_not.why: custom and her own grief both allow some private time before burial, which she has not yet had

then: She holds the child through the morning, then asks for the burial to proceed that same afternoon, before the heat worsens further.
why: The heat makes further delay genuinely harmful and custom itself only grants a short private time rather than an open one, so grief yields to those two pressures together rather than to either alone.
turns_on: how much the heat has already affected the body
